title: A global pandemic in the time of viral memes: COVID-19 vaccine misinformation and disinformation on TikTok
screen_reason: Content analysis of 100 trending TikTok videos from #covidvaccine, coded against CDC-derived categories. Table 1 reports the number and % of videos (and % of cumulative views) in explicitly false content categories - 'Falsely Claims Vaccine Availability for Public Uptake' (31/100), 'COVID is a Hoax' (3/100), 'Vaccine is a Hoax' (3/100) - i.e. quantitative shares of items judged false against an external ground truth.

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok #covidvaccine, English and Spanish videos; falsity judged against US vaccine availability)
estimates.date: Not explicitly stated; collected while no COVID-19 vaccine was yet available in the US (on/before mid-December 2020); manuscript received 23 December 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of trending #covidvaccine TikTok videos that falsely claimed a COVID-19 vaccine was available for public uptake
estimates.denominator: 100 trending TikTok videos identified from the hashtag #covidvaccine (the most popular COVID-19 hashtag at the time, ~73.8 million views)
estimates.definition: Video coded as 'Falsely Claims Vaccine Availability for Public Uptake' - it conveyed that a vaccine was available for uptake when none was available in the US at the time of data collection
estimates.misinfo_def: "Whereas misinformation involves drawing erroneous conclusions about a given phenomenon based on incorrect or incomplete facts, a disinformation campaign involves active effort to spread false information to advance a particular agenda."
estimates.source_quote: Falsely Claims Vaccine Availability for Public Uptake 31 15,195,600 43.00% 2,070,254 38.03% 53,300 44.79%
estimates.page_loc: p. 2375, Table 1, row 'Falsely Claims Vaccine Availability for Public Uptake' (count 31 of 100 videos)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Content categories built from a CDC fact sheet and the authors' prior YouTube COVID-19 vaccine study; one coder (CJ) coded all 100 videos, a second (CHB) coded a 10% random sample; overall kappa = .94 with only six discrepancies across all categories
estimates.moderator_quote: One-hundred trending videos were identified from the hashtag #covidvaccine. At the time of the study, this was the most popular of the COVID-19 hashtags with approximately 73.8 million views. ... Further content categories included if the video highlighted any of the following: the false claim that a vaccine was available for uptake (at the time the data was collected, it was not available in the US)
estimates.notes: Main paper-level misinformation share. Note the sample is trending/most-popular videos on one hashtag, so it is rank-truncated and topical, not a random sample of TikTok. The falsity criterion is time-bound (true availability arrived days later in the US), which is unusually literal misinformation coding.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'Discouraged a Vaccine' 38/100 (39.64% of views) was NOT extracted: it is a sentiment/stance category, not a falsity judgement - a truthful video can discourage vaccination - so it fails the CONTENT test. (2) 'Parody/Meme of an Adverse Reaction' 26/100 (31.85% of views) was NOT extracted: parody is explicitly not a truth judgement here, and satire/humour can be non-deceptive; it is closer to a style code. (3) The by-sentiment sub-shares (22/38 = 57.89% of discouraging videos and 7/36 = 19.44% of encouraging videos falsely claimed availability; 25/38 = 65.79% parody among discouraging videos) are subgroup breakdowns of the extracted headline row, so per the collapse rule only the 31/100 figure is kept. (4) Abstract text says 'Of the 38 videos discouraging the vaccine, 25 (65.79%)' whereas Table 1 gives 26 parody videos overall and Table 2 gives 25 among discouraging + 1 among encouraging - consistent. (5) No CONCENTRATION figure (top X% of videos -> Y% of views) is reported. (6) External poll figures quoted in the introduction (e.g. 'nearly 75% of the American public was familiar with a conspiracy theory... and 25% believed the theory was at least partially true') are cited from Pew, not this study's data, and are excluded per R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a purposive, rank-truncated sample: 100 'trending' videos from the single hashtag #covidvaccine, one non-English/Spanish video excluded and replaced; codebook derived from a CDC fact sheet and the authors' prior YouTube study; one coder coded all videos with a second coder double-coding a 10% random sample, overall kappa = .94 (six discrepancies, none in the falsity categories reported); descriptive statistics plus t-tests and chi-square tests in Excel; authors note small sample and non-generalizability.
rob.item6_quote: Further content categories included if the video highlighted any of the following: the false claim that a vaccine was available for uptake (at the time the data was collected, it was not available in the US), a parody/meme of an adverse reaction, the vaccine development process, and identification of a specific company.
rob.item10_quote: Twenty-two of these 38 videos (57.89%) falsely conveyed that a vaccination was available. These 22 videos received 68.78% of the total views among videos that discouraged the vaccine.
